title: Without Metaphysics: The Poetry of Philip Larkin (Sogang University academic page)

Authorship attributed from the site's host; not independently confirmed.

title: All What Jazz, first edition (Jonkers Rare Books catalogue record)
reliability_notes: Describes a copy of the Faber 1970 first edition of All What Jazz: A Record Diary 1961-68; AbeBooks listings agree (ISBN 0571092403). Trade description, not a library catalogue.

title: Aubade (The Philip Larkin Society, philiplarkin.com)
reliability_notes: Gives the completion date (29 November 1977) and first publication in The Times Literary Supplement, 23 December 1977.

title: Critical opinions (1): Larkin and the difficult subject (Gale Literature Resource Center)
reliability_notes: Independent corroboration that Aubade was begun in 1974, finished in 1977 and first printed in the TLS Christmas issue of 23 December 1977, and was Larkin's last substantial lyric.

title: Lorraine Hansberry (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
reliability_notes: Dates, the Woodlawn basis of A Raisin in the Sun, the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award, the 1961 film's Cannes award, marriage to Robert Nemiroff (1953-64); dates the book of To Be Young, Gifted and Black 1970 and calls the 1969 production a Broadway one, both recorded as discrepancies.

title: Lorraine Hansberry (Encyclopedia.com, compiling Gale's Contemporary Black Biography)
reliability_notes: Freedom (1951-53), the Montevideo peace congress (1952), the 1959 award over plays by O'Neill, Williams and MacLeish, Les Blancs at the Longacre (1970), the Random House 1965 Sidney Brustein, and Baldwin's 1969 introduction.

title: Hansberry, Lorraine: Introduction (Encyclopedia.com, Gale literary criticism entry)
reliability_notes: Critical introduction and principal works: 530 performances of Raisin, its ranking among American classics, the later charge of assimilationism, the 1984 expanded edition, 101 performances of Sidney Brustein, and descriptions of The Drinking Gourd and What Use Are Flowers?; lists the New American Library 1961 edition of Raisin.

title: Lorraine Hansberry (AmericanLiterature.com)
reliability_notes: Used only for her anonymous letters to The Ladder in the late 1950s, the 1963 cancer diagnosis and the description of The Movement (1964); no other source consulted covers these points, so they are treated as provisional.

title: Lorraine Hansberry Biography (Chicago Public Library)
reliability_notes: Corroborates 101 performances and the 12 January 1965 closing of Sidney Brustein, her work on Freedom, and the May 1964 speech that gave To Be Young, Gifted and Black its title.

title: Les blancs: the collected last plays of Lorraine Hansberry (Internet Archive catalogue record)
author_or_editor: Internet Archive (catalogue data from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)

title: Hansberry, Lorraine 1930-1965 (Encyclopedia.com, Gale entry with Leonard R. N. Ashley's 1990 essay)
author_or_editor: Gale / Cengage (compiled); essay by Leonard R. N. Ashley
reliability_notes: Ashley's essay, citing the Dictionary of Literary Biography vol. 7, documents Dore Schary's commission of The Drinking Gourd and describes What Use Are Flowers? as a short television play about the aftermath of nuclear war; principal works list Les Blancs 1970 and The Collected Last Plays 1972.

title: Albert Murray obituary (The Guardian, 23 August 2013)
reliability_notes: Dates (12 May 1916 - 18 August 2013), adoption, meeting Ellison at Tuskegee, wartime service and 1962 retirement, The Omni-Americans' critique of Baldwin, the National Book Critics Circle lifetime achievement award (1996) and the Harper Lee Award (1998).

title: George Orwell bibliography (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Read as raw wikitext (sections on books, pamphlets, editing and collected editions). Dates and publishers of the novels (Animal Farm 17 August 1945; Nineteen Eighty-Four 8 June 1949), the pamphlets (James Burnham and the Managerial Revolution, Socialist Book Centre, July 1946; The English People, Collins, 1947), the edited volumes (Talking to India, 1943; British Pamphleteers vol. 1, with Reginald Reynolds, 1948), the posthumous collections and the collected editions (CEJL, 4 vols; Complete Works, ed. Peter Davison, 20 vols, 1986-1998). Tertiary. Its 1958 date for the American Dickens, Dali and Others conflicts with the bibliographical sources (April 1946) and is not followed.

title: George Orwell Bibliography: Most referenced collections (orwell.ru)
reliability_notes: Critical Essays: Secker and Warburg, London, 14 February 1946, 3,028 copies; American edition Dickens, Dali and Others: Studies in Popular Culture, Reynal and Hitchcock, New York, April 1946. Contents of the later collections. Enthusiast-maintained, but detailed and consistent with library catalogue records.

title: George Orwell published: list of works (orwell.ru)
reliability_notes: Contents of Critical Essays (ten essays), of England Your England and Such, Such Were the Joys (1953), and the six parts of The English People. Two copies of this list (orwell.ru and a mirror) give slightly different contents for the 1953 collections; only items common to both are relied on.

title: Shooting an Elephant and Other Essays, 1950 (orwell.ru library record)
reliability_notes: First published 5 October 1950 by Secker and Warburg; eighteen essays listed with the years of their first publication.

title: Shooting an elephant, and other essays (WorldCat record, OCLC 2552523)
reliability_notes: London: Secker and Warburg, 1950; 212 pages, 19 cm. Its contents note includes an "I Write As I Please" selection between 'Second Thoughts on James Burnham' and 'Confessions of a Book Reviewer', which the orwell.ru list of eighteen essays omits.

title: England, Your England and Other Essays, 1953 (orwell.ru library record)
reliability_notes: Contents of the British collection (ten pieces) and the note that it omitted the school memoir included in the American Such, Such Were the Joys, substituting two excerpts from The Road to Wigan Pier.

title: The English People, 1947 (orwell.ru library record, with Daniel J. Leab's note)
reliability_notes: Collins, London, 1947, print run 26,000; commissioned September 1943 and written in spring 1944 after Animal Farm; publication delayed, and the text updated by the publisher in 1946; six parts listed.

title: The English People (essay) (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: First published August 1947; commissioned September 1943 by W. J. Turner for Collins's Britain in Pictures series, an idea from the Ministry of Information; twenty-five illustrations, eight in colour (Ardizzone, Laura Knight, Lowry, Henry Moore, John Minton, Topolski); Orwell called it 'silly' and 'propaganda' and refused to allow a reprint (citing Rodden 2002). A stub.

title: Second Thoughts on James Burnham (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: First published in Polemic No. 3, May 1946; printed as the pamphlet James Burnham and the Managerial Revolution by the Socialist Book Centre in summer 1946; summary of the argument, and the judgements of Michael Shelden, Christopher Hitchens and Robert Conquest.

title: Such, Such Were the Joys (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Composition (probably drafted 1939-40, revised 1945-46, completed May or June 1948, citing Complete Works vol. XIX); first published in Partisan Review in 1952; first book publication in the Harcourt collection of 1953; summary, the Blake allusion, and the challenges to the account's accuracy.

title: Darcy Moore, Orwell Collection (collector's list of first editions)
reliability_notes: Such, Such Were the Joys, Harcourt, Brace, 26 February 1953; England Your England and Other Essays, Secker and Warburg, 12 November 1953; the title essay in Partisan Review vol. 19, no. 5, September-October 1952. A private collector's list, used for exact dates only.

title: The Freedom of the Press (The Orwell Foundation)
reliability_notes: Full text of Orwell's proposed preface to Animal Farm, with the note that it was first published in the Times Literary Supplement on 15 September 1972 with an introduction by Bernard Crick, and that Ian Angus found the manuscript in 1972.

title: Orwell's Proposed Preface to Animal Farm (Marxists Internet Archive)
author_or_editor: Marxists Internet Archive (transcribed by Jonas Holmgren)
reliability_notes: Transcribed text, dated 1945, published in the TLS on 15 September 1972. States that the typescript was discovered in 1971, against the Orwell Foundation's 1972; the discrepancy is recorded on the work.

title: Nineteen Eighty-Four (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext (lead, plot, appendix, characters) and the rendered writing-and-publication section: Orwell on Jura from May 1946, second draft finished November 1948, manuscript sent to Secker and Warburg on 4 December 1948, first printing of 25,575 copies, Harcourt Brace edition 13 June 1949; Orwell's description of the book as a satire showing the perversions to which a centralised economy is liable.

title: Animal Farm (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext (lead, plot, characters): first published 17 August 1945 by Secker and Warburg; original subtitle A Fairy Story, dropped by the American publisher in 1946; written November 1943 to February 1944; rejected by several publishers including Gollancz; the allegorical identifications (citing Rodden 1999).

title: George Orwell (Dictionary of Literary Biography entry, Gale Literature Resource Center)
reliability_notes: Consulted as a search-result extract only, not the full entry: Critical Essays (Secker and Warburg, 1946) published in New York as Dickens, Dali and Others (Reynal and Hitchcock, 1946); characterisations of 'Boys' Weeklies', 'The Art of Donald McGill' and 'Charles Dickens'.

title: Pastors and Masters (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext: published 1925 by Heath Cranton (citing the British Library catalogue), first-edition title Pastors and Masters: A Study, 126 pages; plot, principal characters, the New Statesman review of 20 June 1925, and Britannica on the dialogue method. Used to correct the installment 9 record, which had dated the novel 1941 and given it an unrelated plot.

title: H. G. Wells (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunks 0-1 of 17 (lead and early life): born at Bromley on 21 September 1866, the fourth child of Joseph Wells, a former domestic gardener who was then a shopkeeper and professional cricketer, and Sarah Neal, a former domestic servant who returned to work as a lady's maid at Uppark; cites David C. Smith, H. G. Wells: Desperately Mortal (Yale University Press, 1986), p. 35, which was not consulted directly. Used to check the parentage in the merged installment 8 record, which replaced the earlier text's 'a professional cricketer's daughter'. Not linked to the record, because installment 8 author records take no cited sources.

title: These Sad But Glorious Days (Yale University Press)
reliability_notes: Publisher's page, seen as a search-result extract: Margaret Fuller, These Sad But Glorious Days: Dispatches from Europe, 1846-1850, edited by Larry J. Reynolds and Susan Belasco Smith, 342 pages, publication date 25 December 1991; the dispatches from England, France and Italy 'reproduced in their entirety for the first time'; the November 1848 attack on the Quirinal, the Roman Republic under her friend Mazzini, the June 1849 French siege. Used to date the collection (the author's bibliography list had 1992) and to correct the installment 8 record.

title: Review of These Sad But Glorious Days (Journal of American Studies)
reliability_notes: Only the review's bibliographic heading was seen (search-result extract): New Haven and London, Yale University Press, 1991, 338 pages, ISBN 0 300 05038 0. Independent corroboration of the 1991 date; the review text was not read.

title: The Nebuly Coat (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext (one chunk): a suspense novel, first edition Edward Arnold, London, 1903; plot (Edward Westray sent to Cullerne to supervise the restoration of Cullerne Minster; the mystery of the claim to the Blandamer title, whose nebuly coat of arms is in the great transept window; the new lord who pays for the restoration and is not what he seems), citing the Leeds Mercury review of 23 November 1903; the Spectator review of 14 November 1903; background (Durham Cathedral; Jacques Heyman on the Chichester tower collapse of 1861); editions (Penguin 1943, OUP 1954 and 1988); the 1965 BBC Home Service adaptation and its cast; A. N. Wilson in the Telegraph, 2004. Used to correct the installment 9 record, which had an invented plot (an architect 'John Easter' at 'Casterbridge' and a cursed embroidered coat) and classed the novel as a ghost story.

title: The Fashion in Shrouds (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunk 0 of 2: a crime novel published in 1938 by Heinemann (London) and Doubleday (New York), the tenth Albert Campion novel, between Dancers in Mourning and Traitor's Purse; full plot summary and character list. The article carries an inline-citations warning; its external links point to the Margery Allingham Society's bibliography and plot summaries, which were not consulted. Used to correct the installment 9 record, whose plot had Valentine Ferris found dead and Georgia Wells a former airwoman, and whose character list included a figure not in the novel.

title: Surfeit of Lampreys (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, both chunks. The article covers the plot, a full character list, the title's allusion to Henry I, and the 1950 London stage adaptation by Owen Howell (citing Lewis 1998, p. 136, and Lachman 2014). It describes a detective novel, the tenth Roderick Alleyn novel, published by the Collins Crime Club and "first published in 1941", and as Death of a Peer in the United States. That date is the London edition: the Ngaio Marsh House bibliography gives Boston 1940 for Death of a Peer. Quotes Bargainnier (1981, p. 98) on Roberta Grey and Routley (1972, p. 149) on the novel; neither book was consulted directly. Used to correct the installment 9 record, whose plot said the family had no obvious motive and implied a family member was the murderer, whose characters included a non-existent "Frieda", and whose form was a genre name.

title: Bibliography of Dame Ngaio Marsh's Published Works
reliability_notes: A selection of Marsh's published work that includes the complete crime novel series, with the place and year of the first US and UK editions of each novel, together with her short fiction, non-fiction, articles and plays (fetched in full). It shows six novels published in Boston or Auckland before London: Death of a Peer (Boston 1940; London 1941 as Surfeit of Lampreys); Death and the Dancing Footman (1941; 1942); Died in the Wool (Auckland 1944; London and Boston 1945); Spinsters in Jeopardy (1953; 1954); Singing in the Shrouds (1958; 1959); and Dead Water (1963; 1964). The installment 9 author record had given the London dates. For Death of a Peer, the date is corroborated by bookseller listings of the Little, Brown first edition of 1940 (search-result extracts only). Lists the 1950 stage version of Surfeit of Lampreys with Owen B. Howell among unpublished plays. Used for the Surfeit of Lampreys record and for the dates, co-author and US titles in Marsh's bibliography.

title: Down and Out in Paris and London (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunks 0-2 of 4. Covers the background (Orwell's tramping from 1927, Paris 1928-29, hop-picking in 1931), the publication history ('A Scullion's Diary', the rejections by Cape and by Faber with T. S. Eliot's letter, Gollancz, the choice of title and pen name, the Harper edition, the 55,000-copy Penguin of December 1940, the 1935 French translation), a chapter-by-chapter summary, 'fact and fiction' and the reception. The publication date is given as both 22 January 1933 (infobox) and 9 January 1933 (text); the record states only the month. Reviews and letters are quoted at second hand. Used for the new installment 9 record (the book had been listed only in Orwell's bibliography).

title: A Clergyman's Daughter (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunks 0-1 of 3. Covers the background (Southwold, the hop-picking journal of 1931, teaching at Hayes in 1932-33), the dates of composition (mid-January to 3 October 1934), publication by Gollancz on 11 March 1935 and in the US in August 1936 as The Clergyman's Daughter, a five-chapter plot summary, the characters, the themes (with Smyer 1975) and criticism, including Orwell's letters disowning the book and Vincent McHugh's review of 1936. Used for the new installment 9 record.

title: Inside the Whale and Other Essays (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, one chunk. A short article: published by Gollancz on 11 March 1940, 1,100 copies, some destroyed by bombing; its contents ('Inside the Whale', 'Charles Dickens', 'Boys' Weeklies'); and the different Penguin collection of 1962 with the same title, a reprint of Selected Essays (1957). Used for the new installment 9 record.

title: Inside the Whale (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunk 0 of 2. The article on the title essay: background (Tropic of Cancer, Orwell's dinner with Miller in December 1936), a part-by-part account of the argument, and extracts, including the 'necessary murder' passage. Used for the summary of the title essay in the new installment 9 record.

title: The Lion and the Unicorn: Socialism and the English Genius (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, one chunk. Covers publication by Secker & Warburg on 19 February 1941 as the first Searchlight Book (series edited by T. R. Fyvel and Orwell), the argument, the three parts, Eileen Blair's description (via D. J. Taylor, 2023) and John Major's speech of 22 April 1993. The article is short and gives no account of each part's argument, so the record does not assign arguments to parts. Used for the new installment 9 record.

title: Malcolm Muggeridge (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunks 0, 3 and 4 of 5: the lead, early life and career, Moscow, and the full list of works; chunks 1 and 2 (later career) were not read. Gives birth at Sanderstead, Surrey, death at Hastings, Selwyn College, teaching at Union Christian College (Kingdom of Cochin) and in Egypt, Moscow in 1932, the anonymous famine reports of 25, 27 and 28 March 1933, Picture Palace (completed January 1933, published 1934 but not distributed), and Winter in Moscow (1934), described only in outline. The list of works has no 'Picture of Mortimer and Ray', and an exact-title web search found only Daniel Pinkwater's unrelated The Picture of Morty and Ray (2003). The installment 9 record of that title was therefore removed as fabricated. The author record had also given the birthplace as Croydon and the place of death as Robertsbridge. Goodreads lists a novel 'Autumnal Face', which the Wikipedia list omits; it is not recorded until verified.

title: Heinemann African Writers Series (Wikipedia), section "Bibliography"
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (chunks 0-9 of 10). The table states that it reproduces the bibliography prepared by Nourdin Bejjit (Open University PhD, 2009) and printed in James Currey, Africa Writes Back (Oxford: James Currey, 2008), pp. 301-310; Currey's book and Bejjit's thesis were not consulted. All numbered entries 1-270 were transcribed except no. 65, which the table omits, together with the 97 unnumbered titles of 1985-2003 and the contributors the table names for anthologies, into research/installment_10/lists/heinemann_african_writers_series_1962_2003.csv (641 rows). Defects found in the table: the note to no. 31 (A Man of the People, 'originally published 1959') conflicts with the novel's 1966 first publication; the 1995 entry credited to Lindsey Collen gives the title, link and 1983 Braziller edition of Buchi Emecheta's The Rape of Shavi; misspellings (Sepho Sepamia, Cosmo Peterse, Musaemura Zimuya, Molara Ogunidpe Leslie, 'Echoing Siliences', 'tradedy'); many entries of the 1970s-1990s leave the genre and, for translated books, the source language blank. Used for discovery only, never as verification of a work.

title: Iowa Writers' Workshop (Post45 Data Collective; Program Era Project)
author_or_editor: Nicholas Kelley, Nicole White and Loren Glass
reliability_notes: Peer-reviewed dataset: people (3,115 students and teachers, 1931-2014, with country of origin and library authority identifiers), graduations (3,051 thesis records with year, degree and genre) and 1,228 works by Workshop authors held by HathiTrust. Only graduates with an LCCN, VIAF or Wikidata identifier (published authors) and the HathiTrust works dated 1946-2000 were used, as discovery evidence for American writing outside the prize and bestseller records.

title: Commonwealth Foundation prizes (Wikipedia), sections on the Commonwealth Writers' Prize and the Commonwealth Short Story Competition
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (chunks 0-6 of 7). The tables cite the Commonwealth Foundation's list of regional winners 1987-2007 (archived PDF, not consulted). All Best Book winners 1987-2000, Best First Book winners 1989-2000 and Short Story Competition winners 1996-2000 were transcribed into research/installment_10/lists/commonwealth_writers_prize_1987_2000.csv (112 rows). Points to check: the country column gives Canada for Olive Senior (1987) and South Africa for Lindsey Collen in 2005 though Mauritius in 1994; 1996 (Best Book) and 1989 (Best First Book) have no African selection; the 1998 short-story winner's title is blank. Used for discovery only.

title: Heinemann Caribbean Writers Series (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (1 chunk). The introduction quotes Anthony van der Vlies in The Oxford Companion to the Book (2010): the series was founded in 1970, modelled on the African Writers Series, and Michael Anthony's The Year in San Fernando was its first title. The table lists only 33 titles, with years of first publication rather than of the series edition, so it is a selection, not a bibliography of the series. Transcribed into research/installment_10/lists/heinemann_caribbean_writers_series.csv (33 rows; the anthology row is credited to its editor). Errors and doubtful entries: Witchbroom (1992) is credited by the table's grouped cell to Vanessa Spence, but Wikipedia's article on Lawrence Scott (seen as a search extract) lists it as his first novel (Allison & Busby, 1992; Heinemann Caribbean Writers Series, 1993), and the CSV credits it to Scott; the table dates Paulette Ramsay's Aunt Jen 1970, but WorldCat (OCLC 51668740) and Google Books, seen as search extracts, record Oxford: Heinemann, 2002, in the Caribbean Writers Series, so the CSV gives 2002 and the title falls outside the inventory; the genre 'Novel' for Michael Anthony's Cricket in the Road comes from a grouped cell and was not checked. Used for discovery only.

title: Sam Selvon (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (2 chunks). Cites Kenneth Ramchand's ODNB entry (2004; not consulted), Louis James's obituary in The Independent (20 April 1994; not consulted) and Michel Fabre's interview in Susheila Nasta (ed.), Critical Perspectives on Sam Selvon (1988), for Selvon's account of writing The Lonely Londoners in dialect. Gives birth and death (20 May 1923, San Fernando - 16 April 1994, Piarco International Airport), the pseudonyms of his Trinidad Guardian years, the Dundee fellowship (1975-77), the move to Canada, two marriages, Guggenheim Fellowships in 1955 and 1968, and a bibliography. Discrepancies with other sources: Turn Again Tiger is dated 1958 in the text and 1959 in the list; Eldorado West One is dated 1988 in the text and 1989 in the list; the list alone includes 'A Meap Story' (1954).

title: The Lonely Londoners (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunk 0 of 2 read (overview, social commentary, narrative technique and the start of the adaptations). Cites Susheila Nasta's introduction to the Penguin edition (2006), Christian Mair in The Journal of Commonwealth Literature 24.1 (1989) and Helon Habila in The Guardian (17 March 2007). First publishers: Allan Wingate (UK) and St Martin's Press (US), 1956, 142 pp.

title: Samuel Selvon: 'The Lonely Londoners' - 1956, by Bill Schwarz (London Fictions)
publisher: Five Leaves (London Fictions, ed. Andrew Whitehead and Jerry White); online at londonfictions.com
reliability_notes: Chunks 0-2 of 4 read (the essay in full; chunk 3 is site navigation). Bill Schwarz is a professor in the School of English and Drama at Queen Mary, University of London. Quotes the opening and closing passages of the novel, discusses the summer section, Galahad's soliloquy on colour and Moses' sense of stasis, and locates the novel's London (Westbourne Grove, Bayswater, the Harrow Road). States that Selvon confirmed T. S. Eliot's influence and read for the BBC's Caribbean Voices. Used for The Lonely Londoners and for Selvon's early years in London.

title: The Lonely Londoners Full Plot Summary (GradeSaver)
author_or_editor: John Melendez; edited by James Cooper
reliability_notes: Last reviewed 29 June 2023. Chunk 0 of 2 read; the remainder (Harris's party, the pigeon, the close) was seen as search-result extracts, including the guide's summary of pp. 101-129. A study guide, not scholarship: used only for the order of episodes and for details of minor characters, which agree with Wikipedia and Schwarz where they overlap. Calls Lewis Tolroy's brother; other accounts make him a brother-in-law, so the record does not state the relationship.

title: Samuel Selvon (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
reliability_notes: Biography read (the AI panel on the page was ignored). Dates Ways of Sunlight 1958 and I Hear Thunder 1962, against 1957 and 1963 in the other sources; places his death in Port of Spain, where Wikipedia has Piarco International Airport; dates his start at the Trinidad Guardian to 1946. Calls Turn Again Tiger 'perhaps his best' and notes its extensive use of dialect.

title: Samuel Selvon, by Kwame S. N. Dawes (EBSCO Research Starters)
reliability_notes: Chunks 0-1 of 3 read (biography, list of works and annotated bibliography). Lists eleven long fictions including 'A Drink of Water' (1968), not listed elsewhere, and omits 'A Meap Story'; dates the Guggenheim Fellowships 1954 and 1968 (Wikipedia: 1955 and 1968); calls his wartime post 'telegraph operator' (Wikipedia: wireless operator); lists writer-in-residence posts at Alberta, Calgary, Victoria, Winnipeg and Dundee; mentions an unfinished novel, 'A High of Zero', and an autobiography in progress at his death.

title: Sam Selvon (South Asian Britain: Connecting Histories)
author_or_editor: Making Britain / South Asian Britain project, University of Bristol and partners
reliability_notes: Chunk 0 of 2 read (biography and published works, with first publishers). Gives his parents (Bertwyn Fraser Selvon; Daisy Irene Dickson), his literary editorship of the Sunday Guardian, more than twenty BBC radio plays, the television scripts Anansi the Spider Man and Home, Sweet India, the script of Horace Ove's Pressure (1976), and his involvement with the Caribbean Artists Movement in the late 1960s. The list of published works is the record's main check for first editions: Allan Wingate (1952-1956), MacGibbon & Kee (1957-1970), Davis Poynter (1972, 1975), Longman (1983, 1989) and Peepal Tree (1988, 1991). Posthumous books outside the period: Poems of Sam Selvon (2012) and Calypso in London (2023).

title: Samuel Selvon (Asian Heritage in Canada, Toronto Metropolitan University Library)
reliability_notes: Chunk 0 of 2 read.
